questions.question: Your frontend can't fetch your API — you get a CORS error. What is happening and how do you fix it?
questions.title: Cross Origin Scenarios
questions.direct_answer: The browser's Same-Origin Policy blocks JS from reading cross-origin responses unless the server opts in. A 'CORS error' means the API response is MISSING the required Access-Control-Allow-Origin header (or it mismatched). The fix is server-side: send Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the specific origin or *), and for non-simple requests handle the OPTIONS preflight with the allow-methods/headers headers. Common mistakes: fixing from the frontend (can't — it's a server contract), credentialed requests with wildcard origin (forbidden), and proxy confusion in dev.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping to fixes without reproducing or measuring first.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[fetch to api.example.com] --> SIM{simple request?}
    SIM -->|yes| REQ[send directly]
    SIM -->|PUT/custom hdr| PRE[OPTIONS preflight]
    PRE --> PO{server allows?}
    PO -->|no| BLK[request never sent - CORS error]
    PO -->|yes| REQ2[real request]
    REQ --> RH{response has ACAO header?}
    REQ2 --> RH
    RH -->|no| BLOCK[browser blocks JS from reading]
    RH -->|yes| READ[your JS gets the response]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why SOP exists (the threat model): the browser attaches your cookies to cross-site requests automatically. Without SOP, any site you visit could run JS that reads your Gmail/intranet/bank — authenticated by your cookies, invisible to you. SOP closes the read-channel by default; CORS is the escape hatch where servers EXPLICITLY opt specific origins into reading. This is why CORS can never be 'fixed' client-side — the contract is between browser and server, and your JS is the thing being protected against.

The preflight design (why OPTIONS exists): the spec splits requests into 'simple' ones browsers could already send before CORS (GET, POST with form encodings, limited headers — historically safe) and 'new capability' ones (PUT/DELETE, JSON bodies, auth headers). For the new ones, the browser asks permission first — because a non-simple request can mutate server state, and SOP's original guarantee was that cross-site JS couldn't do that. Preflight caching (Access-Control-Max-Age) exists because the OPTIONS round-trip otherwise doubles request latency for every call.

The adjacent mechanisms worth distinguishing (the follow-ups): cookies + CORS (credentials mode, SameSite interplay — SameSite=Lax blocks most cross-site cookie sends, narrowing CORS-with-credentials cases); postMessage (the sanctioned cross-frame/channel API — different mechanism, same trust question: always validate event.origin); and CORS vs CSRF (CSRF rides requests the browser SENDS regardless of read-permission — CORS is about reading responses, CSRF is about triggering actions; the mitigations differ: CSRF needs SameSite/tokens, CORS needs headers).
